reader_summary: This section asks whether extra computation at answer time is worth its cost. I can follow the artificial budget: one 80-token answer plus five verification tokens costs 85, while four 20-token answers plus five verification tokens each cost 100. The model weights stay fixed while the answering procedure changes. To compare procedures, I would record final accuracy, whether any candidate contains the answer, selection failures, and actual cost under an explicit budget. The cited 24-question experiment used different total generation budgets, so its modest coverage/majority improvements do not identify the best equal-budget procedure. I understand the distinction among generated-token counts, measured batch-generation time, full user-request latency, and the earlier training/evaluation/saving cost. I cannot fully interpret the table's token accounting phrase “包含EOS” because this section and the linked material I needed do not define EOS.

issues.location: The paragraph introducing the k/token/time table: “實際生成總token，包含EOS”
issues.details: EOS appears without expansion or a plain explanation. The counting rule matters to this cost comparison; a first-time reader cannot tell what additional kind of token is included or why it is counted. The consulted sampling section 1.15 does not define it, and 16.3 mentions EOS as a structure ID without explaining its role.
issues.requested_change: At first use, add a short definition, for example “包含EOS（表示生成結束的專用token，也計入生成數量）”. Then the table's accounting boundary is understandable without looking elsewhere.

background_and_links.details: I first read all of C.5, then its named C.3 and C.4 prerequisites. C.3 explains token, candidate count k, and coverage; C.4 separates selection accuracy from coverage and explains arithmetic verification. C.3 itself gives enough of the short-answer versus visible-step training example to understand the two table columns, so I did not need C.1. I consulted C.3's linked 1.15 for sampling, which clarified temperature/generation but not EOS. I consulted C.5's linked 16.3 for the limited cache idea and batch definition. Basic multiplication/probability and C.4's self-contained 2+2 verifier made W.4 and C.2 unnecessary for this section. I did not follow the deeper neural-network links because C.5 needs only the cache/time-cost idea, not their implementation.

terminology.details: Test-time compute is explained as extra computation during answering, and weights are described as training-adjusted numerical values. C.3 defines token; C.3/C.4 define coverage, candidate k, and majority/verification selection. Attention is briefly described in C.5; the linked 16.3 shows that cache preserves prior K/V work and defines batch as several sequences processed together. “Latency” is grounded in the start-to-finish request interval, and cold start is separated from an already running service. EOS remains undefined at the token-accounting rule and is the sole open readability issue.

examples.details: I can reproduce 80+5=85 and 4*20+4*5=100 by hand. In the cited experiment, k is candidates per question, each row aggregates 24 questions, short answers allow at most 8 new tokens per candidate, and step answers allow 48. The k=8 step coverage goes from 11/24 to 14/24, while majority final accuracy goes from 11/24 to 12/24. Step token totals 512 versus 4,132 are approximately eightfold; the text expressly avoids claiming an equal-budget optimum. The lower short-answer time at k=8 is presented as a single-run observation affected by batching/execution order, not a reliable speed ranking. I did not reproduce any cited model results or the 45.71-second experiment cost.

program_explanation.details: The fenced program has a list named plans; each entry maps candidate count and answer length to numbers. verify_tokens_each is five. The for loop visits each plan, assigns n from candidates, computes generated=n*answer_tokens_each and verified=n*verify_tokens_each, then prints their sum. I predicted the exact two lines and ran this original fence in an offline CPU Python process; the outputs matched 85 and 100. It performs arithmetic only: it neither generates answers nor measures accuracy or elapsed time. Its supported conclusion is that equal answer-generation totals can have unequal generation-plus-verification totals.

exercise.details: I saved my prediction before executing: changing only verify_tokens_each from 5 to 0 makes verified zero for both plans, leaves both generated counts at 80, and prints totals 80 and 80. I made exactly that edit in my artifact copy and executed it; both lines matched. I can explain why zero added model tokens does not imply zero CPU verification time, better four-candidate accuracy, or equal waiting time. The final instruction to use real fixed-test-question results for a quality curve marks work beyond this arithmetic exercise.
